Variants.Content: A noble feast is both for eating and drinking and a place for openly displaying order. Who sits closest to the high seat, which house has a place on the dais, and who must share a bench with knights or squires are all read as honor or slight; the number of courses, the vintage of the wine, and who receives the first toast likewise convey favor and wealth. Feasts serve well for sealing betrothals, sounding out allies, and spreading news, and carry a sacred air of protection through guest right. Kitchens, minstrels, servants, and guards keep the great hall running, and they often hear far more than the highborn at table suppose. A single slight in seating can become a new name for an old grievance.

When nobles enter a great hall, they look first to the seating and only then to the food. Being placed a step farther from the high table may be a steward's blunder, or a chill the host meant for all the hall to see.

Merchants and craftsmen see a feast as orders and connections: wine, cloth, silver plate, and spices can all be turned into coin. An invitation to sit at table brings respectability, yet may also require repaying a favor the next day.

Servants and the poor see how many families the leavings of a feast could feed, while septons remind the host of the laws of hospitality and alms. The more lavish the hall within, the harder it is to claim that the hunger outside the gates goes unknown.
